questions.stem:
An 18-year-old college freshman has 6 days of fever to 39.8 C (103.6 F), severe sore throat and fatigue. Examination shows enlarged tonsils covered with white exudate, swelling around both eyes, enlarged posterior cervical lymph nodes and a palpable spleen tip. Labs show:

[[labs 0]]

The large lymphocytes on his smear are best described by which of the following?
choices: Infected B cells that have entered the blood through the CD21 receptor
Cytotoxic CD8 T cells responding to virus-infected B cells
Plasma cells secreting heterophile antibody against foreign red cells
Natural killer cells that have lost control of viral replication
Infected epithelial cells shed from the inflamed oropharynx

explain.html:
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) enters through the oropharynx, where it replicates in epithelial cells, and then infects B cells through the CD21 receptor. The infected B cells provoke an intense cytotoxic T-cell response, and those activated CD8 T cells are the atypical lymphocytes that define primary EBV mononucleosis. The infected B cells also make heterophile antibodies, mostly IgM, against antigens on foreign red cells. So the virus lives in the B cells, but the large cells on the smear are the T cells attacking them.

This freshman has the full picture of infectious mononucleosis: high fever, exudative tonsillitis, periorbital edema, posterior cervical nodes, a spleen tip and raised transaminases. His lymphocytosis with large cells full of cytoplasm is that CD8 response, and the same T-cell control is what normally keeps EBV in check for life.
why: The virus does enter B cells through CD21, but the infected B cells are not the large cells seen on the smear.
Heterophile antibody is made by infected B cells, and antibody-secreting cells are not what the atypical lymphocytes are.
Failure of T and NK cells to control EBV describes the lymphoproliferative complications, not the usual mono smear.
Oropharyngeal epithelial cells are where EBV first replicates, but they do not circulate in blood.
explain.takeaway: The atypical lymphocytes of EBV mononucleosis are cytotoxic CD8 T cells reacting to B cells that EBV infected through CD21.
explain.topic: EBV: cell tropism and atypical lymphocytes
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Explain the clinical presentations of EBV and CMV infections in normal hosts and those with altered host defenses

rows.if_right: a child with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis or X-linked lymphoproliferative disease after primary EBV

questions.stem:
A 46-year-old man received a liver transplant 7 months ago and takes high-dose immunosuppressive drugs after an early rejection episode. He now has fever, weight loss and enlarged lymph nodes in the neck and abdomen. Biopsy of a node shows sheets of B cells, and in situ hybridization detects viral nucleic acid in nearly all of them. Before transplant he was seropositive for a herpesvirus that 90% of US adults carry.

Which of the following best explains how the virus persisted to cause this disorder?
choices: It persisted as a circular episome in B cells, maintained by nuclear antigens
It integrated into hepatocyte DNA and was spread by the transplanted liver
It persisted in bone marrow stem cells and later reactivated as a high-level viremia
It was shed in the urine for years and later reinfected lymph nodes
It persisted in sensory ganglia and traveled down nerves to the nodes

explain.html:
Like the other herpesviruses, EBV establishes lifelong latency in B cells after primary infection, and those cells are the reservoir. The latent genome sits in the nucleus as a circular episome, and the few proteins made during latency include the EBV nuclear antigens (EBNA), which keep the episome maintained. Cytotoxic T cells normally keep those B cells in check. Heavy immune suppression removes that control, and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder follows, ranging from a benign polyclonal B-cell proliferation to a malignant B-cell lymphoma.

This liver recipient was EBV seropositive before transplant (about 90% of US adults are), is on intensified immune suppression, and has nodes full of B cells carrying viral nucleic acid. The risk tracks the degree of immunosuppression and is highest in the first year after transplant, which is exactly where he is.
why: EBV latency is in B cells as an episome, not integrated into hepatocyte DNA, and the tumor here is made of B cells.
Latency in bone marrow stem cells is how cytomegalovirus persists, and it would not explain a B-cell tumor.
Prolonged shedding in urine describes cytomegalovirus, and shedding does not create a B-cell proliferation.
EBV does not hide in sensory ganglia; its reservoir is the B cell.
explain.takeaway: EBV persists as an EBNA-maintained episome in B cells, and loss of T-cell control after transplant lets those cells proliferate, with the highest risk in the first year.
explain.topic: EBV latency and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Explain the clinical presentations of EBV and CMV infections in normal hosts and those with altered host defenses

rows.why: EBV latency is in B cells as an episome, not integrated into hepatocyte DNA, and the tumor here is made of B cells.
rows.if_right: a virus whose latent reservoir is the liver itself

rows.why: Latency in bone marrow stem cells is how cytomegalovirus persists, and it would not explain a B-cell tumor.
rows.if_right: a transplant patient with viremia and end-organ disease from a beta-herpesvirus

rows.why: Prolonged shedding in urine describes cytomegalovirus, and shedding does not create a B-cell proliferation.

rows.if_right: a painful dermatomal vesicular rash from varicella zoster reactivating out of sensory ganglia

questions.stem:
A 7-year-old boy from rural equatorial Africa, where malaria transmission is intense year round, presents with a rapidly enlarging mass of the jaw over 3 weeks. Biopsy shows sheets of medium-sized B cells with a very high proliferation rate. Nearly every tumor cell carries the genome of a herpesvirus that latently infects B cells. Cytogenetic study shows a translocation that places a growth-promoting gene next to an immunoglobulin locus.

Which gene is most likely involved in this translocation?
choices: embB
c-myc
rpoB
katG
inhA

explain.html:
EBV is an oncogenic virus, and each EBV-linked cancer pairs the virus with a cofactor in a particular at-risk group. Transplant lymphoproliferative disease and primary CNS lymphoma in AIDS ride on immune suppression, nasopharyngeal carcinoma clusters in southern China and the Inuit with genetic and dietary cofactors, and Hodgkin lymphoma has a variable link. Endemic Burkitt lymphoma in African children is over 95% EBV associated, and its cofactors are malaria and a c-myc translocation.

This boy from a malaria region has a fast-growing jaw mass of highly proliferative B cells carrying EBV, and the translocation puts a growth gene beside an immunoglobulin locus. That gene is c-myc. The other choices are mycobacterial drug-resistance genes and have nothing to do with a B-cell tumor.
explain.table:
EBV-linked cancerAt-risk groupCofactor
Lymphoproliferative diseaseTransplant recipientsImmune suppression
Primary CNS lymphomaAIDS with low CD4Immune suppression
Nasopharyngeal carcinomaSouthern China, InuitGenetic and dietary
Endemic Burkitt lymphomaAfrican childrenc-myc translocation, malaria
why: embB is a mycobacterial gene, not a growth gene moved next to an immunoglobulin locus.
rpoB is a mycobacterial gene, not a human oncogene in a B-cell tumor.
katG is a mycobacterial gene and plays no part in Burkitt lymphoma.
inhA is a mycobacterial gene and plays no part in Burkitt lymphoma.
explain.takeaway: Endemic Burkitt lymphoma is an EBV-driven B-cell tumor of African children with malaria and a c-myc translocation as cofactors.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Explain the clinical presentations of EBV and CMV infections in normal hosts and those with altered host defenses

questions.stem:
A 24-year-old graduate student has had 3 weeks of fever, fatigue and malaise. She has no sore throat and no tonsillar exudate, and her lymph nodes are only slightly enlarged. Her leukocyte count is normal with 18% atypical lymphocytes, and her ALT is 140 U/L (7 to 56). A heterophile antibody test is negative twice, and serology shows prior, not recent, Epstein-Barr virus infection. She works part time in a daycare center.

Which virus is the most likely cause of her illness?
choices: Adenovirus
Human parainfluenza virus
Norovirus
Influenza B virus
Cytomegalovirus

explain.html:
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is ubiquitous and spreads by direct contact with secretions, and most normal hosts have no symptoms. When adolescents and adults do get sick, the typical picture is a heterophile-negative mononucleosis-like illness with prolonged fever, atypical lymphocytosis and hepatitis. Pharyngitis and big nodes are less prominent than in EBV mono. Even healthy people shed CMV in urine, saliva and genital secretions for months to years, so young children are a steady source.

This student has 3 weeks of fever, atypical lymphocytes and an ALT of 140 with little sore throat, two negative heterophile tests and serology showing only past EBV. Her daycare job puts her next to the children who shed CMV. That combination points to CMV rather than a respiratory or GI virus.
explain.table:
EBV mononucleosisCMV mono-like illness
Heterophile testPositive (adolescents, adults)Negative
Sore throat, exudateProminent, often severeMinor
Atypical lymphocytesYesYes
Hepatitis, prolonged feverCommonThe main features
why: Adenovirus causes pharyngitis, conjunctivitis and respiratory illness, not weeks of fever and hepatitis with negative heterophile tests.
Parainfluenza causes croup, bronchiolitis and upper respiratory illness in children.
Norovirus causes abrupt vomiting and diarrhea that resolves in 1 to 4 days.
Influenza causes abrupt fever, myalgia and respiratory symptoms over days, not weeks of atypical lymphocytosis and hepatitis.
explain.takeaway: CMV in a healthy adolescent or adult causes a heterophile-negative mono-like illness with prolonged fever, atypical lymphocytosis and hepatitis.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Explain the clinical presentations of EBV and CMV infections in normal hosts and those with altered host defenses

rows.why: Adenovirus causes pharyngitis, conjunctivitis and respiratory illness, not weeks of fever and hepatitis with negative heterophile tests.
rows.if_right: a child with fever, pharyngitis and conjunctivitis after a swimming pool outbreak

rows.why: Parainfluenza causes croup, bronchiolitis and upper respiratory illness in children.
rows.if_right: a toddler with a barking cough and stridor

rows.why: Norovirus causes abrupt vomiting and diarrhea that resolves in 1 to 4 days.
rows.if_right: a cruise ship outbreak of vomiting and non-bloody diarrhea

rows.if_right: an abrupt winter illness with fever, myalgia and cough

questions.stem:
In July, 14 children who attended the same summer day camp develop fever, sore throat, red watery eyes without purulent discharge and tender cervical lymph nodes. All of them swam in the camp's public pool, which a later inspection found was poorly chlorinated. Camp staff who did not swim are unaffected. Testing of a throat swab by PCR identifies a small, non-enveloped double-stranded DNA virus.

Which feature of this virus best explains how the outbreak spread?
choices: Its outer lipid envelope protects it from drying out on wet pool surfaces
Its lack of an envelope lets it survive in water and on surfaces
Its segmented genome allows rapid exchange with animal strains
Its latency in B cells allows lifelong shedding into pool water
Its strict winter seasonality concentrates cases in swimmers

explain.html:
Adenoviruses are small non-enveloped double-stranded DNA viruses with more than 80 types. Without a lipid envelope they are hardy: they spread through respiratory secretions, aerosols and fomites and survive on environmental surfaces, while enteric strains spread fecal-orally. They have no definite seasonality and cause outbreaks in military recruits, college campuses, long-term care residents and around public swimming pools. The classic syndrome is pharyngoconjunctival fever: fever, pharyngitis, a benign conjunctivitis and cervical adenitis.

These campers have exactly that syndrome, it hit only the children who swam in a poorly chlorinated pool, and PCR found a small non-enveloped dsDNA virus. The virus's lack of an envelope is what lets it survive in pool water and on wet surfaces long enough to infect the next swimmer.
why: Adenovirus has no envelope, and an envelope makes a virus more fragile, not less.
A segmented genome describes influenza; adenovirus has a single dsDNA genome.
Latency in B cells describes EBV, which spreads in saliva, not through pool water.
Adenovirus has no definite seasonality, and this outbreak happened in July.
explain.takeaway: Adenovirus is a hardy non-enveloped dsDNA virus that survives in water and on surfaces and causes pool-linked pharyngoconjunctival fever.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand the epidemiology and diverse clinical manifestations of Adenovirus infections

rows.why: Adenovirus has no envelope, and an envelope makes a virus more fragile, not less.
rows.if_right: an enveloped virus, which would be expected to die quickly outside the body

rows.why: A segmented genome describes influenza; adenovirus has a single dsDNA genome.
rows.if_right: a new influenza strain arising after co-infection of a pig

rows.why: Latency in B cells describes EBV, which spreads in saliva, not through pool water.
rows.if_right: a teenager with mono after kissing an infected partner

rows.why: Adenovirus has no definite seasonality, and this outbreak happened in July.
rows.if_right: a virus that causes annual winter epidemics, such as RSV

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old previously healthy man had abrupt fever, chills, headache and severe myalgias 8 days ago, followed by a cough. His fever resolved on day 5 and he began to feel better. On day 7 he developed a new high fever, rigors and a cough productive of thick sputum. Chest radiograph shows a dense right lower lobe consolidation with cavitating areas, and sputum Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters.

Which of the following best explains his worsening?
choices: Primary viral pneumonia from continued influenza replication
Secondary bacterial pneumonia caused by Staphylococcus aureus
Reye syndrome from salicylates taken for his fever
Reactivation of latent tuberculosis that was triggered by the recent influenza
Myositis of the respiratory muscles with rising creatine kinase

explain.html:
Influenza starts abruptly with fever, chills, rigors, headache and myalgia, and respiratory symptoms and cough take over as the systemic illness fades. Its complications split into respiratory and non-respiratory groups. Pneumonia can be primary viral or secondary bacterial, caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus. Non-respiratory complications include myositis with high creatine kinase (especially influenza B), Reye syndrome in children given salicylates, myocarditis and Guillain-Barre syndrome.

This man had classic influenza, improved by day 5, then spiked a new fever with thick sputum. A dense consolidation with cavitation and Gram-positive cocci in clusters identify secondary S. aureus pneumonia. The biphasic course is the clue that a bacterial superinfection, not the virus itself, caused the turn for the worse.
why: Primary viral pneumonia continues the first illness and would not show clustered Gram-positive cocci after a period of recovery.
Reye syndrome is a liver and brain complication in children given salicylates, not a lung consolidation in an adult.
Nothing in the history points to tuberculosis, and clustered Gram-positive cocci are not mycobacteria.
Influenza myositis causes tender leg muscles and a high creatine kinase, not a cavitating consolidation.
explain.takeaway: Improvement followed by new fever and productive cough after influenza signals secondary bacterial pneumonia from S. pneumoniae or S. aureus.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand the concept of antigenic drift and antigenic shift and the presentation and complications of Influenza infection

rows.why: Primary viral pneumonia continues the first illness and would not show clustered Gram-positive cocci after a period of recovery.
rows.if_right: worsening hypoxia without a break in the illness and no bacteria on sputum stain

rows.why: Reye syndrome is a liver and brain complication in children given salicylates, not a lung consolidation in an adult.
rows.if_right: a child on aspirin during influenza who develops encephalopathy and liver failure

rows.why: Nothing in the history points to tuberculosis, and clustered Gram-positive cocci are not mycobacteria.
rows.if_right: months of cough and weight loss with acid-fast bacilli on sputum

questions.stem:
A 70-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease comes to the emergency department in January with 2 days of abrupt fever, chills, myalgias and a worsening cough. Several residents of her assisted living facility have had a similar illness this week. A rapid influenza antigen test on a nasal swab, which returns in 30 minutes, is negative. Her clinician still suspects influenza.

Which of the following is the best interpretation and next step?
choices: The negative test excludes influenza, so she needs only bacterial cultures
Repeat the rapid antigen test in 7 days, when viral shedding has peaked
Send paired serology 2 weeks apart, the gold standard for acute diagnosis
The rapid test is sensitive but nonspecific, so a positive test was expected
The rapid test is specific but insensitive, so send a real-time RT-PCR

explain.html:
Influenza cannot always be told apart from other respiratory viruses on clinical grounds, so testing matters. Real-time RT-PCR is the gold standard, run on nasopharyngeal aspirates, nasopharyngeal swabs or nasal swabs. Rapid antigen tests return in 30 to 60 minutes and are specific but less sensitive, so a positive result is trustworthy while a negative one does not exclude influenza. Yield is highest when specimens are collected in the first few days of illness, during peak viral shedding.

This woman has an abrupt January illness, an outbreak in her facility and a negative rapid test on day 2. The negative result cannot rule out influenza, so the next step is RT-PCR now. She also falls in several treatment target groups (65 or older, chronic lung disease, resident of a care facility), which makes the answer matter.
why: A rapid antigen test is not sensitive enough for a negative result to exclude influenza.
Shedding peaks in the first few days, so waiting a week lowers the yield.
RT-PCR, not paired serology, is the gold standard, and serology two weeks apart is too slow to guide care.
This reverses the test: rapid antigen tests are specific but insensitive.
explain.takeaway: Rapid influenza antigen tests are specific but insensitive, so a negative result in a suggestive case should be followed by RT-PCR, the gold standard.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand the concept of antigenic drift and antigenic shift and the presentation and complications of Influenza infection

rows.if_right: a highly sensitive test such as RT-PCR coming back negative

rows.why: Shedding peaks in the first few days, so waiting a week lowers the yield.
rows.if_right: a specimen taken in the first few days of illness, when shedding actually peaks

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old woman who delivered a baby 9 days ago develops abrupt fever, myalgias and cough. Nasal swab RT-PCR detects influenza A. She is started on an oral drug that is a sialic acid analog. In cell culture, influenza-infected cells exposed to this drug still assemble new virions at their surface, but the virions stay clumped on the cell membrane instead of spreading to neighboring cells.

Which viral function does this drug block?
choices: Attachment of hemagglutinin to sialic acid receptors on host cells
Initiation of viral messenger RNA synthesis by the polymerase
Exchange of gene segments between co-infecting strains
Uncoating of the viral genome after entry into the endosome
Cleavage of sialic acid by viral neuraminidase to release progeny virus

explain.html:
Influenza leaves an infected cell by budding, and the new virions stay tethered to sialic acid on the cell surface until neuraminidase cleaves the sialic acid and releases them. The neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir, zanamivir, peramivir) are sialic acid analogs that competitively inhibit neuraminidase, so they interfere with release of progeny virus and work against influenza A and B. Baloxavir acts at a different step, inhibiting initiation of viral mRNA synthesis, and is approved for uncomplicated influenza from age 5.

This woman is 9 days postpartum, which puts her in a treatment target group (pregnant or within 2 weeks of delivery). In the experiment, virions still assemble but stay clumped on the membrane, which is precisely what blocking neuraminidase looks like.
explain.table:
DrugMechanismSpectrum or use
Oseltamivir, zanamivir, peramivirSialic acid analogs that inhibit neuraminidase, blocking release of progeny virusInfluenza A and B
BaloxavirInhibits initiation of viral mRNA synthesisUncomplicated influenza, age 5 and older
why: Attachment by hemagglutinin is not blocked; the cells were infected and made new virions.
Inhibiting initiation of viral mRNA synthesis is how baloxavir works, not a sialic acid analog.
Segment exchange is the mechanism of antigenic shift, not a drug target.
Uncoating is not the blocked step, since new virions were assembled.
explain.takeaway: Neuraminidase inhibitors are sialic acid analogs that block release of progeny influenza A and B virions; baloxavir blocks initiation of viral mRNA synthesis.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand the concept of antigenic drift and antigenic shift and the presentation and complications of Influenza infection

rows.if_right: virus that never enters the cells in the first place

rows.why: Inhibiting initiation of viral mRNA synthesis is how baloxavir works, not a sialic acid analog.
rows.if_right: a drug that stops the virus from making any new viral proteins

questions.stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department at 2 AM in the fall with a harsh, barking cough and a high-pitched noise on inspiration that started tonight. He had 2 days of runny nose and low-grade fever. He is alert and drinking, with inspiratory stridor at rest that improves when he calms down in his mother's arms. Neck radiograph shows narrowing of the subglottic trachea.

Which virus is the most common cause of this illness in his age group?
choices: Respiratory syncytial virus
Human parainfluenza virus types 1 and 2
Human parainfluenza virus type 3
Adenovirus
Influenza B virus

explain.html:
The human parainfluenza viruses (HPIV) are enveloped, negative-sense single-stranded RNA paramyxoviruses with five types, each with its own epidemiology. HPIV-1 and HPIV-2 are the most common cause of croup in children 1 to 5 years old. HPIV-3 is endemic and causes mainly bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants under 1. HPIVs also account for a large share of childhood upper respiratory infections and otitis media, and in stem cell transplant recipients they can cause refractory pneumonia.

This 2-year-old has a cold followed by a barking cough, inspiratory stridor that settles when he calms and subglottic narrowing, which is croup. At his age that points to HPIV-1 or HPIV-2. Treatment is symptomatic in a normal host, and no vaccine exists because immunity is not durable.
explain.table:
VirusMain syndromeTypical age
HPIV-1 and HPIV-2Croup1 to 5 years
HPIV-3Bronchiolitis, pneumoniaUnder 1 year
RSVBronchiolitis, pneumoniaInfants, especially premature
why: RSV mainly causes winter bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants, not croup in a toddler.
HPIV-3 mainly causes bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants under 1.
Adenovirus can cause croup but is not its most common cause.
Influenza is not the usual cause of croup.
explain.takeaway: Croup in children 1 to 5 is most often caused by parainfluenza types 1 and 2, while parainfluenza type 3 causes bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Know the common presenting signs and symptoms of Human parainfluenza viruses

questions.stem:
On day 3 of a cruise in February, 120 passengers develop sudden nausea, forceful vomiting, watery non-bloody diarrhea and cramps, many with low-grade fever and myalgias. Most recover within 2 days. Cases continue despite alcohol-based hand sanitizer dispensers at every dining room entrance. Stool PCR identifies a small non-enveloped single-stranded RNA virus in the calicivirus family.

Which measure would best address the reason cases continue?
choices: Handwashing with soap and water, since the virus resists alcohol
Starting all passengers on a neuraminidase inhibitor
Cooking shellfish thoroughly, since food is the only route
Isolating passengers for 24 hours, since shedding ends with symptoms
Air filtration, since the virus spreads only by droplet nuclei

explain.html:
Noroviruses are non-enveloped single-stranded RNA viruses in the calicivirus family and are the most common cause of gastroenteritis in all age groups. They are highly infectious and spread several ways at once: fecal-oral person-to-person spread, contaminated food and water, droplets from vomitus, and surfaces where they persist for days. Illness begins 12 to 48 hours after exposure with abrupt vomiting, non-bloody diarrhea and cramps and resolves in 1 to 4 days, but virus can be shed in stool for 4 weeks. Because the virus has no envelope, prevention relies on hand hygiene with soap and water, not hand sanitizer, plus environmental disinfection and disposal of contaminated material.

This cruise outbreak keeps going despite alcohol sanitizer at every entrance, which is exactly what a non-enveloped virus would do. Soap and water handwashing addresses the gap.
why: Neuraminidase inhibitors treat influenza and have no effect on norovirus.
Food is only one route; person-to-person, vomitus and surface spread continue regardless of cooking.
Norovirus can be shed in stool for weeks after symptoms end, so 24 hours of isolation does not stop spread.
Norovirus spreads mainly fecal-orally, by surfaces and by vomitus droplets, not only through the air.
explain.takeaway: Norovirus is a non-enveloped calicivirus that resists alcohol, persists on surfaces and is shed for weeks, so outbreaks are controlled with soap and water and disinfection.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand the clinical signs/symptoms of Norovirus

rows.if_right: a single common-source outbreak traced to one batch of shellfish

questions.stem:
A 3-month-old girl born at 28 weeks' gestation, who has chronic lung disease of prematurity, is seen in December with 3 days of runny nose followed by fast breathing, wheezing and poor feeding. Oxygen saturation is 89% on room air, and she has diffuse crackles and wheezes. Nasal PCR detects an enveloped, non-segmented negative-strand RNA virus whose fusion protein lets it enter airway epithelial cells. Her mother asks what could protect her next infant.

Which statement about this infection and its prevention is correct?
choices: A live vaccine given at birth is the standard way to prevent it
The virus spreads mainly through contaminated food and water
A first infection gives lifelong immunity, so reinfection does not occur
A monoclonal antibody given to the infant can prevent infection
Oral neuraminidase inhibitors are the standard preventive drug

explain.html:
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is an enveloped, non-segmented negative-strand RNA virus; its G protein attaches to the cell and its F (fusion) protein lets it penetrate airway epithelium. It spreads by close contact with secretions, large droplets and fomites in winter and early spring epidemics. About 20 to 30% of infected infants develop bronchiolitis or pneumonia, and hospitalization concentrates in infants born before 29 weeks, those with chronic lung disease of prematurity, certain congenital heart disease, immunodeficiency and neuromuscular conditions. Most children are infected by age 2, and reinfection occurs but is milder. Antibodies against F and G are protective, which is the basis of prevention.

This 28-week preterm infant with chronic lung disease has December bronchiolitis from RSV. For her next sibling, nirsevimab, a monoclonal antibody, prevents infection in babies, and a separate product is given to pregnant people at 32 to 36 weeks.
why: No live vaccine at birth is the standard; prevention is a monoclonal antibody for the baby or a product given in pregnancy.
RSV spreads by close contact with secretions, large droplets and fomites, not food and water.
Reinfection with RSV does occur; later infections are milder, not prevented.
Neuraminidase inhibitors are influenza drugs and are not used for RSV prevention.
explain.takeaway: RSV causes winter bronchiolitis, most severe in premature infants and those with chronic lung or heart disease, and nirsevimab (a monoclonal antibody) prevents infection in babies.
explain.topic: RSV in infants: risk and prevention

questions.stem:
A 3-year-old girl in a daycare center has 9 days of fever, exudative tonsillitis, enlarged cervical lymph nodes and an enlarged spleen. Her blood smear shows many atypical lymphocytes. A rapid heterophile antibody test is negative. Her pediatrician still suspects the virus that infects B cells through CD21 and wants to confirm an acute infection.

Which result would best confirm acute infection in this child?
choices: Positive heterophile test on repeat testing in one week
Positive antibody to nuclear antigen, with no capsid IgM
IgG antibody to viral capsid antigen, with nuclear antigen antibody
IgM antibody to viral capsid antigen, with no nuclear antigen antibody
A rising titer of antibody against the patient's own red cells

explain.html:
EBV testing starts with the heterophile antibody, an IgM made by infected B cells that reacts with antigens on foreign red cells. It predicts acute EBV with high sensitivity and specificity in teenagers and adults, but not in children younger than 4, who often do not make it. When the heterophile test is negative and EBV is still suspected, EBV-specific serology dates the infection. IgM to viral capsid antigen peaks in the first 2 to 6 weeks and fades over 2 to 3 months, capsid IgG appears early and lasts for life, and antibody to EBV nuclear antigen (EBNA) appears late and marks past or latent infection.

This 3-year-old has fever, exudative tonsillitis, nodes, a big spleen and atypical lymphocytes, so a negative heterophile test at her age does not exclude EBV. Capsid IgM without EBNA antibody is the pattern of a new, acute infection.
explain.table:
EBV testWhen it is positiveWhat it means
Heterophile antibodyAcute illness, adolescents and adultsAcute EBV, unreliable under age 4
Viral capsid antigen IgMPeaks weeks 2 to 6, gone by 2 to 3 monthsAcute infection
Early antigen IgGEarlyAcute infection
Viral capsid antigen IgGEarly, then lifelongInfection at some time, does not date it
EBNA antibodyLate, then lifelongPast or latent infection
why: Heterophile antibodies are unreliable under age 4, so a repeat heterophile test cannot confirm EBV in her.
Nuclear antigen antibody appears late and marks past infection, and capsid IgM is absent.
Capsid IgG lasts for life and EBNA antibody marks past infection, so this pair points to an old infection.
Heterophile antibodies react with foreign red cells, not her own, and are unreliable at her age anyway.
explain.takeaway: Heterophile antibodies miss acute EBV in children under 4; viral capsid IgM without EBNA antibody confirms acute infection.

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old man had an allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant 2 months ago, complicated by graft-versus-host disease treated with high-dose steroids. He now has fever, a dry cough and hypoxemia. Chest CT shows bilateral ground-glass opacities. Bronchoalveolar lavage and blood PCR both show a high viral load of a beta-herpesvirus. His team starts an intravenous drug whose first phosphorylation is carried out by an enzyme encoded by the virus.

Which laboratory value should be monitored most closely on this drug?
choices: Serum uric acid
Serum creatine kinase
Leukocyte and platelet counts
Serum potassium
QT interval on ECG

explain.html:
In immune suppressed patients CMV causes either CMV syndrome (fever, malaise, cytopenias and viremia without tissue invasion) or CMV disease with end-organ damage. The usual organ depends on the setting: enteritis after kidney transplant, and pneumonitis after stem cell transplant (especially with graft-versus-host disease) and lung transplant. Treatment is to reduce immune suppression and give a drug that targets CMV DNA polymerase. Ganciclovir is a nucleoside analog whose first phosphorylation is done by a virus-encoded enzyme and the rest by cellular enzymes, so the active drug builds up more than tenfold in infected cells.

This stem cell recipient with GVHD on steroids has ground-glass pneumonitis and a high beta-herpesvirus load, and he is on IV ganciclovir. Myelosuppression is the most important toxicity of ganciclovir and its oral prodrug valganciclovir, so leukocyte and platelet counts are what to watch.
why: Uric acid is not a ganciclovir toxicity; myelosuppression is the one that matters.
Creatine kinase rises with influenza myositis, not with ganciclovir.
Potassium is not the toxicity named for ganciclovir.
QT prolongation is not a ganciclovir toxicity.
explain.takeaway: CMV pneumonitis is the classic end-organ disease after stem cell transplant with GVHD, and ganciclovir (first phosphorylated by a viral kinase) is limited mainly by myelosuppression.
explain.topic: CMV in transplant recipients and ganciclovir

questions.stem:
A novel influenza strain spreads rapidly worldwide. Sequencing shows that its hemagglutinin gene segment came from an avian strain while its other segments came from a human strain, after a pig was co-infected with both. Almost no one in the population has antibody against the new hemagglutinin. In the same year, a research group studies an influenza B lineage that has accumulated point mutations in its hemagglutinin over several seasons.

Which statement correctly contrasts the two strains?
choices: Both strains arose by antigenic shift, but only the B strain can cause pandemics
The novel strain arose by antigenic drift, which is restricted to influenza A
The B strain arose by antigenic shift, which produces an entirely new subtype
The novel strain arose by antigenic shift, which occurs only in influenza A
Both strains arose by antigenic drift, the main source of pandemic strains

explain.html:
Influenza viruses carry 8 segments of negative-sense single-stranded RNA, and their surface hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) are the main targets of protective immunity. Antigenic drift is a continuous series of point mutations in HA (and less often NA) in both influenza A and B; antibody against the old strain works progressively less well, and drift drives seasonal epidemics. Antigenic shift is an abrupt, major change in which the virus acquires a new genome segment for HA (alone or with NA), creating a new subtype. Shift occurs only in influenza A and can cause a pandemic if the new strain spreads efficiently person to person.

The novel strain picked up an avian HA segment in a co-infected pig and meets a population with no antibody, which is shift. The influenza B lineage changed by point mutations over several seasons, which is drift.
explain.table:
Antigenic driftAntigenic shift
Genetic changePoint mutations in HA (less often NA)New HA segment acquired (alone or with NA)
Influenza typesA and BA only
SpeedGradual, continuousAbrupt, major
ResultSeasonal epidemicsNew subtype, possible pandemic
why: Influenza B does not undergo shift, and only shift can produce pandemics.
Drift occurs in both A and B, and the novel strain arose by segment exchange, not point mutations.
Point mutations accumulated over seasons are drift, and influenza B cannot undergo shift.
Only the B lineage drifted; pandemics come from shift, not drift.
explain.takeaway: Antigenic shift (a new HA segment by reassortment) happens only in influenza A and can cause pandemics, while antigenic drift (HA point mutations) happens in A and B and causes seasonal epidemics.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand the concept of antigenic drift and antigenic shift and the presentation and complications of Influenza infection

rows.if_right: an influenza A strain that acquired a new HA segment

rows.why: Drift occurs in both A and B, and the novel strain arose by segment exchange, not point mutations.
rows.if_right: a strain that changed only by point mutations in HA over several seasons

rows.why: Point mutations accumulated over seasons are drift, and influenza B cannot undergo shift.
rows.if_right: an influenza A strain that gained a new HA from an avian virus

rows.why: Only the B lineage drifted; pandemics come from shift, not drift.
rows.if_right: two strains that both changed only by gradual HA point mutations

questions.stem:
A 12-year-old boy who received a hematopoietic stem cell transplant 6 weeks ago develops fever, painful urination and gross hematuria. Urine bacterial culture is negative and platelet count is adequate. The next week he becomes jaundiced, and a liver biopsy shows areas of necrosis with intranuclear inclusion bodies. PCR of urine and blood detects the same virus, which is also a common cause of conjunctivitis and pharyngitis in healthy children.

Which of the following best describes this virus?
choices: An enveloped negative-sense RNA virus that is treated with inhaled ribavirin in severe cases
A beta-herpesvirus that is first phosphorylated by a viral kinase
A non-enveloped double-stranded DNA virus that is diagnosed by tissue, culture or PCR
A calicivirus that resists alcohol and is spread only by the fecal-oral route
A segmented RNA virus that causes worldwide pandemics through antigenic shift

explain.html:
Adenoviruses cause different syndromes depending on age and immune status. In healthy children they cause respiratory illness and the classic pharyngoconjunctival fever, and other syndromes include keratoconjunctivitis, gastroenteritis, acute hemorrhagic cystitis, myocarditis and fetal hydrops. They are important pathogens in organ and stem cell transplant recipients, where they can cause severe hepatitis, and a liver biopsy showing necrosis with intranuclear inclusion bodies is characteristic. The virus is a small non-enveloped double-stranded DNA virus, and diagnosis is by histopathology, culture or PCR.

This stem cell recipient has hemorrhagic cystitis with a sterile urine culture, then hepatitis with inclusion-body necrosis, and PCR finds the same virus in urine and blood. A virus that also causes conjunctivitis and pharyngitis in healthy children is adenovirus.
explain.table:
VirusStructureSignature in this lecture
AdenovirusNon-enveloped dsDNAPool conjunctivitis, hemorrhagic cystitis, inclusion-body hepatitis in transplant
CMVEnveloped dsDNA herpesvirusPneumonitis or enteritis in transplant, treated with ganciclovir
ParainfluenzaEnveloped negative-sense RNACroup; ribavirin in severe immune compromised pneumonia
NorovirusNon-enveloped ssRNA calicivirusVomiting and diarrhea outbreaks, resists alcohol
Influenza ASegmented negative-sense RNAPandemics through antigenic shift
why: This describes parainfluenza virus, which causes respiratory disease, not hemorrhagic cystitis and inclusion-body hepatitis.
This describes CMV, but the stem's virus also causes pharyngitis and conjunctivitis in healthy children and has inclusion-body hepatitis with cystitis.
This describes norovirus, which causes vomiting and diarrhea, not cystitis and hepatitis.
This describes influenza A, a respiratory virus that does not cause hemorrhagic cystitis.
explain.takeaway: Adenovirus, a non-enveloped dsDNA virus, causes hemorrhagic cystitis and necrotizing hepatitis with intranuclear inclusions in transplant recipients and is diagnosed by histology, culture or PCR.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Understand the epidemiology and diverse clinical manifestations of Adenovirus infections
